83e11856f5fe60b705d41b8313518ac0.text: Linda Lou Howarth and Ivy Bowe where at this month's Bewitching Market in Williams Lake selling frybread and fry dawgs to support Howarth and her husband to go to Las Vegas in December where their grandson, and Bowe's great-nephew, Tanner Loring will be competing in the Junior National Finals Rodeo. Linda Lou Howarth of Tatla Lake, located west of Williams Lake, couldn’t be more proud of her grandson as she continues to sell homemade breads and buns to be able to watch him compete in Las Vegas at the upcoming YETI Junior National Finals Rodeo (NFR). Tanner Loring, 16, of Riske Creek is one of more than 700 young cowboys and cowgirls who will be heading to the entertainment capital of the world in December after qualifying for novice bull riding. In Williams Lake at the Bewitching Market on Saturday, Oct. 10, Linda could be found with Tanner’s great-aunt Ivy Bowe selling fresh frybread and fry dawgs. Sales that evening went towards paying for Linda and her husband, Loring’s grandfather, flight to Vegas to watch their grandson. “When I heard he was going to Vegas, I just hit every market I could to sell bread, and I’m doing quite well,” Linda said, adding that when her grandson is on television, she’s glued to the screen. In addition to the Bewitching Market, Linda also baked bread and buns to sell at various markets throughout the area over the summer. Bella Coola was where she was most successful with her sales, supporting their travel to Las Vegas. She has raised over $2,000. “We’re quite excited,” Linda said, adding she was able to watch Tanner compete in the B.C. Rodeo Association’s (BCRA) POLARIS Championship Finals Rodeo held at the 77th North Thompson Fall Fair & Rodeo in Barriere. Loring was crowned BCRA Champion in junior steer riding, with Reese Colgate of Williams Lake also crowned BCRA Champion in junior breakaway roping. Burning is expected to begin on Sunday, Oct. 18 and may continue periodically until Oct. 31. A prescribed burn to help restore natural forest health is anticipated to begin on Sunday, Oct. 18 in the Siwash area, approximately 100 kilometres west of Williams Lake. In a joint information bulletin by the Ministry of Forests and BC Wildfire Service (BCWS), burning may continue periodically until Oct. 31 on approximately 112 hectares of land west of Yunesit’in and southwest of Alexis Creek. Motorists travelling along Highway 20 are advised smoke and flames will be visible. The ignitions of forest fuels within pre-established boundaries to help control mistletoe infestations within the forest stand will only proceed with favourable weather and atmospheric venting, allowing smoke to clear quickly. 375467a093490920e992ffa0c494dd9e.text: A fall storm will bring mixed weather conditions to the multiple B.C. regions on Saturday, Oct. 17, according to Environment Canada. A little bit of nearly every kind of weather is expected on Saturday, Oct. 17 in the Eastern Fraser Valley, Okanagan, and Cariboo regions, including the Coquihalla Highway (Hope to Kamloops), Okanagan Connector, and Highway 3 (Hope to Princeton via Allison Pass), prompting Environment Canada to issue a special weather statement on Friday morning. The only area not impacted is the Chilcotin area, including Kamloops and Ashcroft. According to the government weather agency, a fall storm is going to bring mixed weather conditions, including heavy winds. “A sharp cold front moving across the B.C. Interior on Saturday will primarily generate strong gusty winds of 60 to 80 km/h,” stated Environment Canada. “Ahead of this cold front, strong southwest winds gusting to 80 km/h will develop lee of the Coast Mountains in the Chilcotin this morning.” Additionally, the cold front and unstable air could generate scattered showers, small hail and risk of thunderstorms across the central interior and parts of the Columbia regions. The weather could result in localized power outages, fallen branches, slippery conditions for drivers. High profile vehicles should also take caution in the high winds, added Environment Canada.

d6f7103a27358f395185ad968c97c674.text: The Kelowna RCMP is alerting the public to an ongoing telephone scam following an increase in reports involving fraudsters who are spoofing the detachment's non-emergency phone number, 250-762-3300. Individuals across Canada are receiving calls from someone alleging to be an RCMP officer, and the number appears to originate from the Kelowna detachment’s legitimate non-emergency line. These calls are a phone scam, where the fraudster appears genuinely connected to the Kelowna RCMP, in order to deceive individuals into providing sensitive personal and financial information. After receiving a significant number of reports from people claiming to have received fraudulent calls from the Kelowna RCMP non-emergency line, police are alerting the public to an ongoing scam involving fraudsters spoofing the detachment’s non-emergency phone number, 250-762-3300. According to Cpl. Allison Konsmo, the fraudulent caller falsely identifies themselves as an RCMP officer and claims police have a person in custody who is allegedly in possession of their personal information. “The caller then attempts to persuade the victim to click on a link and provide sensitive information, including passwords, account details, and other personal information,” said Cpl. Konsmo. • Request that you provide financial information to secure your accounts. “These calls are not originating from the Kelowna RCMP, despite what may appear on caller ID,” said Cpl. Konsmo. “We want to remind the public that caller ID information can be manipulated and should not be relied upon as proof of who is calling.” Anyone who receives one of these calls is encouraged to hang up immediately and avoid engaging with the caller. If you are unsure whether a call from police is legitimate, disconnect and contact your local police agency using a publicly listed phone number. If you are a victim of fraud, please contact the Kelowna RCMP non-emergency line at 250-762-3300. For more information on fraud or to report an incident

A grand jury in Washington State indicted the alleged co-conspirator in the fatal Tumbler Ridge mass shooting, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office. James Cody Bryant, 30, was indicted Wednesday (Oct. 14) by a grand jury sitting in the Western District of Washington for conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country for Bryant’s alleged role in the school shooting that left seven people, including the shooter, dead at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School on Feb. 10. The charge is specific to the school shooting. Shooter Jesse Van Rootselaar also shot and killed her mother and brother before going to the school. An indictment by a grand jury is a necessary step in the U.S. federal criminal justice system, where the grand jury determines whether there is enough evidence to even seek a trial for the charge. The indictment says that Van Rootselaar used an improvised explosive device to damage the school and tried to get into other classrooms by firing through locked doors. The shooter exchanged gunfire with the police, but ultimately died from a “self-inflicted wound.” Acting United States Attorney Neil Floyd first announced the charge against Bryant, a Bellingham resident, on Oct. 6. Bryant, who is transgender, has been identified by other media as using the name Melody. Conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country can come with a sentence of up to life in prison. The charge against Bryant has not yet been proven in court. Bryant, who was denied bail on Tuesday, is scheduled for arraignment on Oct. 22. The indictment alleges “several overt acts” Bryant is accused of to “further the school shooting conspiracy.” The indictment alleges that as early as August 2025, Bryant agreed to record the shooting and broadcast it over the internet. In communities across British Columbia, sport is about much more than competition. It’s where children build friendships, volunteers bring neighbours together, and families gather at local arenas, fields, pools and recreation centres. But for too many families, particularly in smaller and rural communities, the opportunity to participate is becoming increasingly difficult to afford. As British Columbians prepare to vote in municipal and provincial elections, affordability is understandably dominating the conversation. Yet one important consideration risks being overlooked: whether families can afford to keep their children involved in sport, and whether their communities have the facilities and resources to make participation possible. In many parts of regional B.C., the challenges are particularly acute. A young hockey player may have to travel hours for games or practices. A family whose child participates in swimming, soccer or basketball may face significant transportation and accommodation costs simply because local programs or facilities are unavailable. Registration fees, equipment and tournament expenses add to the financial pressure. For families with more than one child, those costs can quickly become overwhelming. And while larger centres may offer multiple facilities and programs, smaller communities often depend on a single arena, aging recreation centre or limited number of playing fields. When facilities require major repairs, or programs cannot attract enough coaches and volunteers, opportunities can disappear. These are not simply recreation issues. They are questions of affordability, community health and the future of smaller communities. Sport BC believes the next provincial government, along with newly elected municipal councils, has an important opportunity to address these challenges. 9e3d0f6820392a4bb73871d67067d676.text: Conservative candidate for Juan de Fuca-Malahat Mike Hicks was under fire Friday for saying at an Oct. 9 debate that First Nations must be “conquered.” Hicks said in an interview that he meant that, by law, if a First Nation is unconquered, treaties must be negotiated. “In law, as I understand it, English law, you can’t just move into an area and take it over; you either have to conquer the First Nations in a war or sign a treaty,” he said. “And we did neither. We just moved in and settled in B.C. “And we have to negotiate the treaties. And I’m all for it, of course.” Because a moderator cut him off after he said “First Nations have to be conquered,” it appeared as though he advocated for conquest. “That’s been misconstrued because people have just taken the part that was cut off,” he said. “I guess that’s the game I’m in,” he said. “It’s very disheartening.” Dana Lajeunesse, the NDP candidate for the riding, released a statement condemning Hicks’s choice of words. “Mike Hicks’s attempts to explain away his comments miss the point,” Lajeunesse said. “The word ‘conquered’ carries a long and painful history, and regardless of the point he was trying to make, there is no place for that kind of language today.” Green Party Leader Emily Lowan called on the Conservatives to remove Hicks from the party slate. “This isn’t one bad moment. It’s a pattern,” Lowan said in a news release. This is just one of three separate controversies that erupted in less than 24 hours over candidate posts, comments or professional behaviour. As early voting began on Friday, the provincial political campaign seemed to be shifting away from policy and toward mudslinging. The string of accusations began on Thursday afternoon, when the Conservative Party removed Vancouver-Strathcona candidate Jordan McIntosh after accusations that he posted Holocaust-minimizing statements on social media under a pseudonym. 897de4354d862676885acf365b902ef8.text: CentreBC leader Elenore Sturko and Langley-Walnut Grove candidate Kyle Stevenson were in Langley Friday, out front of Walnut Grove Secondary, for an education platform announcement. CentreBC leader Elenore Sturko said, during a visit to Langley on Friday, Oct. 16, that her party would provide permanent spaces for 25,000 more students in B.C. public schools. She said the new classroom spaces will be in place by 2031, with the districts with the most portables and fastest growth targeted first. “We’ll keep class size and class composition limits in teachers contacts and fund them fully,” Sturko said. Among her promises was to bring back letter grades for students from Grade 4 and up, to give a clear picture of student progress to parents. She also promised to add 1,500 education assistants to B.C. classrooms, fund behaviour support teams in every district, and bring in 350 child- and youth-care workers and behaviour specialists. Sturko also said school food programs would expand to 40 per cent of B.C. students by 2030. The CentreBC leader also pledged more school counsellors, and extending early reading screening-style programs to math as well. She said her party could pay for their educational plan while returning the province’s books to balance. “Unlike the other parties, we actually have a path to balance in two terms,” she said, calling the incumbent NDP government’s deficit spending a “payday loan.” Joining Sturko Friday were four of her regional candidates – Kyle Stevenson from Langley-Walnut Grove, Parm Bhandol from Surrey North, Paul Brar from Surrey-Fleetwood, and Sargy Chima from Surrey-Cloverdale. Langley and Surrey have seen rapid growth of young families, and have disproportionately seen portable classrooms sprout up outside schools. BC Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson addresses media in Port Moody on Friday, Oct. 16, 2026. BC Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson addresses media in Port Moody on Friday, Oct. 16, 2026. BC Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson says the money saved by building a bridge to replace the aging George Massey Tunnel would pay for construction of a new hospital for women and children south of the Fraser. At a press conference in Port Moody Friday morning (Oct. 16), Doerkson expanded on the previous day’s press release wherein the party committed to scrapping the planned eight-lane replacement tunnel in favour of a 10-lane “George Massey Bridge,” completing the Surrey Hospital in Cloverdale (which is already underway and set to open in early 2030), and building a new women and children’s hospital in Surrey. Thursday’s press release claimed a bridge would cut current commute times by up to 30 minutes and help businesses move goods more efficiently, but did not provide any specifics for how much the new bridge would cost, or when it might be complete. In August of 2021, the BC NDP government announced the Fraser River Tunnel Project, a new toll-free eight-lane immersed-tube tunnel featuring one dedicated transit lane in each direction and a separate multi-use path to support walking, biking and other active transportation options. The crossing, to be located immediately upstream of the 65-year-old George Massey Tunnel, came with a $4.15-billion price tag (updated in July 2026 to $8.5 billion) and an estimated completion date in late 2030 (changed this year to September 2031). Doerkson said Friday building a new bridge would cost $6 billion and take five years to build, adding it would be “more affordable” and could be “completed more quickly.” The $2.5 billion saved over the cost of a new tunnel would be used to fund construction of the new women and children’s hospital.
